newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Business leaders compile APEC action plan.
newsitem.headline: Business leaders compile APEC action plan.

text.p: Top Asia-Pacific business executives, impatient with the slow pace of regional trade liberalisation, urged APEC members on Thursday to clear away obstacles to the movement of both people and capital.

Representatives of the APEC Business Advisory Council (ABAC) presented their proposals in a report to Philippine President Fidel Ramos, who will host this year's summit of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum on November 25.
Ramos, who has said one of his goals as chairman was to give the private sector a heightened role in APEC, immediately announced that the Philippines would adopt at least two of the recommendations.
The first involved introducing a five-year, multiple-entry visa for APEC business travellers and the setting up of APEC business lanes at airport immigration counters.
The second involved convening a round-table forum where representatives of the private sector, government and financial institutions can discuss infrastructure needs.
"I am impressed with the practicality of the flagship recommendations (of ABAC)," Ramos said.
"This is what APEC needs -- practical suggestions for policies that can be delivered by governments in a reasonably short period," he added.

ABAC chairman Roberto Romulo later told a news conference that group members believed APEC's goals of trade and investment liberalisation by 2010 for developed members and 2020 for the less well-off should be brought forward.
"All of us ... believe we should move at a faster pace than we are moving at the moment," said Romulo, chairman of Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co and Ramos's former foreign minister.
Apart from reducing immigration hassles for business travellers, ABAC also urged the harmonisation of regional customs procedures to speed up the flow of goods and services.
It also proposed rewarding countries which provide a liberalised investment environment by providing them with cheaper financing for specific projects.

To qualify for this, countries would have to undertake not to nationalise these projects, to honour contracts and to allow the firms involved to choose their own personnel. The project should also enjoy equal access to domestic markets and resources.
Romulo said private and multilateral lending institutions could then offer cheaper financing in return. He added that details of this arrangement still had to be worked out.

The proposals also include a series of round table discussions to focus on the region's massive infrastructure needs and the setting of a network to give small- and medium-scale enterprises better access to markets and credit.

ABAC member Timothy Ong, managing director of Brunei's National Insurance Co, said ultimately the test of what the group recommended would be if it benefited even the poorest communities in the region.
"The main thrust of the ABAC report is how we can spread the prosperity we see in the successful economies of the region into the other economies," Ong said.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, China, Chile, Hong Kong, Japan, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, South Korea, Singapore and the United States.
